A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TelecomTS, and their complete main texts, appendices, tables, figures, and equations support comparison. Retained material can be matched despite substantial layout changes and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original 5G measurements, synthetic anomaly generation, and model evaluations for detection, localization, root cause analysis, forecasting, and question answering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds multimodal model results, controlled scale ablations, and reasoning-trace analyses.

M1.justification: v2 adds a reasoning-trace synthesis pipeline using metadata conditioning, rejection sampling, and composite scoring (Appendix F). It also introduces Toto+Qwen3-4B models with encoder pre-alignment, LoRA fine-tuning, and reasoning supervision, plus NME scale-encoding adaptations. These are procedural and architectural additions; the original measurement and synthetic-anomaly pipelines largely remain.

E1.justification: The limited extension is reasoning-supervised training and qualitative assessment of reasoning outputs for existing anomaly and network Q&A tasks. The underlying 5G scenarios, applications, KPIs, and fault coverage remain unchanged. Recasting existing anomaly tasks as Q&A and reporting windowed sample counts do not establish new measurement coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 2–4 and 6 add Toto+Qwen-3-4B and its +Thinking variant. Table 5 adds DLinear and per-KPI linear regression. Mantis without scaling and additional scale-aware variants provide further evaluated comparisons. The original comparator families are retained.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the normal/anomalous evaluation ratio from 95/5 to 80/20 while retaining 1,000 samples. The reported training schedule changes from learning rate 0.0001, batch size 64, and 10 epochs to 0.001, 32, and 5 epochs. New multimodal training stages and scale controls are introduced. These documented revisions do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 directly tests scale information through Mantis component removal and NME additions across five architectures and six tasks (Section 4.6, Table 7). Appendix F adds candidate-versus-selected trace-score analysis and diagnostic reasoning examples. The original forecasting failure examples are retained and relocated, rather than constituting new experiments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports benchmark uncertainty through repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new trace-score distributions and quantiles describe candidate quality, rather than uncertainty in benchmark performance estimates.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces scores under the revised class mix, including Mantis F1 changing from 0.711 to 0.800; this is not a same-setting gain. Table 4 changes FEDformer accuracy from 0.355 to 0.495 and Informer from 0.600 to 0.654, alongside revised reported training settings. Substantial new results cover multimodal models, classical forecasting baselines, scale ablations, and trace selection. Most retained Table 3 and language-model Table 6 results remain equivalent after rounding or percentage conversion.

T1.justification: Appendix F.1 adds mathematical definitions of the composite trace-selection score and its weighted reasoning and format components, including task-specific correctness scoring (Equations 1–3). Neither version provides theoretical guarantees or proofs, and the existing anomaly-generation mathematics is retained.

C1.justification: The introduction adds explicit reasoning annotations supporting reasoning-aware training and evaluation, and the abstract broadens benchmarking to multimodal foundation models. The central claims about de-anonymized observability data, difficult temporal dynamics, and the importance of absolute scale remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking scale to fault discrimination and location inference, discusses optimization and reasoning-capacity tradeoffs, and expands forecasting mechanisms in Appendix H. It also asserts generalizability beyond the testbed and insensitivity to anomaly-duration priors. Appendix F.2 newly claims performance gains from reasoning training, although Tables 2–4 and 6 show lower scores for +Thinking than its non-thinking counterpart.

D1.justification: New appendices document trace-generation models, conditioning metadata, scoring weights, filtering, training stages, and LoRA settings. v2 also clarifies corpus counts, revises the sample schema, and discloses that forecasting includes normal and anomalous sequences. The printed direct dataset URL disappears while the code URL remains; this establishes an access-information change, not loss of dataset availability.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting reasoning training, early fusion, anomaly prevalence, and specific telecommunications fault mechanisms, including Parker, Zhang, Chameleon, and ADBench. Some earlier references, including citations for retained time-series baselines, disappear. The principal positioning against anonymized and normalized observability datasets remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative is edited and condensed while retaining its overall organization. Q&A curation absorbs the separate statistics subsection, the closing discussion is reorganized, and forecasting discussion moves to Appendix H. Training details move from Appendix F to G after the new reasoning appendix; much of the original appendix prose remains intact.

P2.justification: v2 converts the main text and references from single-column to two-column presentation and extensively rearranges displays. Table 1 is restructured, benchmark tables gain rows, Figure 5 is revised, and Table 7 plus reasoning-quality Figures 17–18 are added. The original forecasting Figure 7 becomes Appendix H Figure 19.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its central scale claim mainly through comparisons between different models; v2 adds direct component-removal and scale-addition controls, substantially strengthening that evidence. Trained multimodal comparisons and detailed reasoning-data procedures also improve the benchmark's usefulness and reproducibility. The reasoning contribution remains less convincing: validation uses the selection score itself, and Appendix F.2 claims gains despite lower +Thinking results. These weaknesses qualify the additions but do not outweigh the stronger experimental support for the paper's central contribution.
